extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and storytellers seeking to write immersive settings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating immersive, story-serving settings in fiction by using time/location, viewpoint-specific detail, sensory specificity, and purposeful scene-level choices to develop tone, character and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and Location (space/place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is made up of Time and Location (also referred to as space or place). Both Time and Location are critical points of information a reader needs to help ground them in your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly provide when and where a scene occurs so readers are grounded. Consider geography, seasons, historical period, and shifts in time/space when the story moves across locations or spans. Use these elements intentionally depending on the kind of story you want to write.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present setting through the viewpoint character
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is always a part of your viewpoint character’s experience. This means that no matter where your story takes place, we should become familiar with that location/time through your viewpoint character’s unique understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filter descriptions through the viewpoint character’s personal worldview and language so even familiar places feel specific and character-driven. Describe settings the way your viewpoint character would describe them to avoid an 'authorly' voice and to make the scene feel lived-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to establish tone and mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting can be used to create tone and mood from one page to the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose sensory details, lighting, weather, architecture, and cultural cues that evoke the emotional atmosphere you want. Small consistent details can shift tone across scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to underscore and amplify tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting can reflect or amplify tension in any given scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select or highlight elements of the environment that mirror or heighten interpersonal or internal conflict (e.g., a claustrophobic room, a leaking roof, a crowded platform). Let the environment contribute to the stakes and unease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to develop plot and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is a wonderful tool to help develop your plots and deepen your characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have setting inform characters’ goals, limitations, backstories, or decisions. Use locations as catalysts for action or as obstacles that shape character arcs and plot movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to provide context and worldbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting helps to bring a deeper understanding of your story world through context and depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed cultural norms, local architecture, social rituals, and small community details to explain how the world works without heavy exposition. Provide context that matters to characters’ choices and the story’s conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ a variety of setting components (culture, architecture, weather, props, senses, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aside from location and time, components such as culture, architecture, weather, other characters, animals, props, and senses expand and deepen setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix these components in scenes to prevent setting from being merely backdrop. Use sensory detail (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste) and props/people/animals to make spaces feel three-dimensional and lived-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every scene’s setting must have a purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask: 'What is my setting’s purpose—not just in the overall arc of the story, but in every scene?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the setting in each scene answers why the character is there now and how the place advances plot, reveals character, sets tone, foreshadows, or creates obstacles. Avoid setting that exists only to be decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid description for description’s sake; inject meaning and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible, avoid description for the sake of description because it’s usually not active. Start with description, and then inject that description with meaning and emotion to give your readers a sense of how important this scene is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn list-like detail into emotionally or narratively charged detail by tying it to character perception, memory, desire, or danger. Make readers feel what the viewpoint character feels so description propels rather than stalls the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific — choose unique, clear, immersive details
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific details create a unique setting that can only exist in YOUR story world. You don’t want to just give your readers any old town park that could mimic all other town parks in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace general, non-specific nouns (house, tree, room, car, town, clothing, food, weather, person, noise) with concrete, distinctive particulars that reveal character and place. Exercise: highlight bland nouns in a page and swap them for vivid specifics that reflect the viewpoint character’s experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twist expectations, plant foreshadowing and motifs in setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask how a familiar location defines character or can be TWISTED to reveal something unexpected, set tone, foreshadow future events, or symbolize theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commonplace settings (e.g., kitchen) in surprising ways to subvert reader assumptions, plant hidden details for later payoff, and use recurring images or motifs in the environment to reinforce theme and trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch out for heavy background, backstory, description, and narrative summary that harm momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Background and backstory are necessary, and description/narrative summary deepen understanding, but heavy setting used incorrectly can become unwieldy and slow things down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance setting detail with action and pacing; avoid long blocks of static description that stop character movement. The correct amount depends on genre and reader expectations—when in doubt, consult a reader familiar with your genre to find the right balance.
